title: He washes their feet (John 13:1–17)
hook: the teacher kneels with a towel and washes twelve pairs of dusty feet

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jar of perfume, a year's wages poured out on his feet. Your line was love can be lavish. Did you give the compliment? Today, feet again, and this time he's the one kneeling. Day sixty-four.

The bathroom nobody cleans. The trash bag that's leaking. The diaper at three in the morning. Every house has jobs that wait for someone else. Tonight's scene is a room in Jerusalem, before the feast of the Passover. Roads were dust and dirt, and sandals don't keep much out. In the Bible, washing feet is servant's work; in the book of Samuel, Abigail offers to do it as a handmaid. John mentions no servant here. He says that during supper, their teacher stands up from the table. Today, he washes their feet.
screen: `THE JOBS NOBODY WANTS.` → `DUSTY ROADS, OPEN SANDALS.` → `THE TEACHER STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: John opens the scene with a line about love, in the King James Bible: "having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end." Then Jesus gets up from supper, lays aside his outer clothes, and ties a towel around his waist, dressed like a servant. "After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded." He goes around the room. One pair of feet after another. Including the feet of Judas, who's about to betray him. Then he comes to Peter, and Peter can't bear it: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." And Peter, all or nothing as always, swings the other way: "Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head." Afterward Jesus puts his clothes back on, sits down, and asks: do you know what I've done to you? You call me master and lord, and you're right. "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." I've given you an example. Later that night he gives them a new commandment: love one another, as I have loved you. In Latin, commandment is mandatum, and the name Maundy Thursday, the Thursday before Easter, is said to come from it. On that day some churches still wash feet, and popes have knelt with a basin too. Among the Brethren, some Mennonites and others, foot washing is part of the communion service. The one who ends up with a crown of thorns starts the night with a towel.
screen: `HE LOVED THEM UNTO THE END.` · `A TOWEL AROUND HIS WAIST.` · `PETER: NEVER MY FEET.` · `MANDATUM: MAUNDY THURSDAY.` · then, large: `YE ALSO OUGHT TO WASH ONE ANOTHER'S FEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe slowly. Picture the basin going around the room, one pair of feet after another. Now think of one humble task waiting for you today. The dishes someone else left. The bin nobody takes out. The coffee pot. The shared bathroom. The email thread nobody wants to answer. Choose one. Plan to do it without saying anything. No announcement, no hint, no post. If anyone asks, just shrug. If you pray, you can offer it quietly. The bell holds the time.
He washes their feet. The teacher kneels with a towel and a basin, even at the feet of the one who will betray him.
Your line: the towel is the crown. Today, do one humble task without mentioning it, to anyone, ever. Day sixty-four.

howItsDone: On Maundy Thursday, the Thursday before Easter, many Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant churches wash feet during the service. Some traditions, including many Brethren and Mennonite churches, practice foot washing regularly with communion.

fork.setup: you're Peter. your teacher kneels in front of you with a basin and a towel to wash your feet. what do you say?
options: you shall never wash my feet.
fork.reveal: Peter refuses: thou shalt never wash my feet. Jesus says, if I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me, and Peter asks for his hands and head too.

original.note: Greek: a linen towel, borrowed from the Latin linteum. The cloth Jesus tied around his waist.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice gesture before dinner.
what it means: the teacher takes a servant's lowest job, washes every pair of feet, including the betrayer's, and tells them to do the same.
what a scholar hears: mandatum, the new commandment of John 13:34, gave Maundy Thursday its name, and the towel, lention, is a Latin loanword, from linteum, a linen cloth.

notes: The index hook says 'twelve pairs of dusty feet'; the text does not count them, and the script does not give a number. Judas's presence: John 13:2, 13:11, 13:26–30.
'The night before Passover': John dates the supper before the Passover feast (13:1); the Synoptics present it as a Passover meal. Addressed in day 65 notes.
Maundy from Latin mandatum (John 13:34, 'mandatum novum'); confirm.

Foot washing on Maundy Thursday (Catholic Mass of the Lord's Supper, Orthodox rite in cathedrals and monasteries, many Anglican and Protestant churches); as an ordinance among Brethren, many Mennonites, Primitive Baptists and others. Confirm.
The closing line of the teach ('crown of thorns ... towel') is the writer's image tying to the carry; the crown of thorns is John 19:2.

Fresh review (days 57–74): John never says there was no servant or that 'nobody picks up the basin'; the hook no longer says so, and the servant's-work point now rests on 1 Samuel 25:41. Cut the banned 'Think of' opener, 'one of the most tender lines in the Gospels' and 'the Pope does it, and so do many bishops'; the Maundy etymology is given as 'is said to come from'; the trapdoor no longer calls lention 'a servant's apron'.
